title: Act III, Scene V
focus: Hecate and the machinery of fate

teacherSummary.text: Hecate angrily scolds the Witches, 'beldams' who are 'saucy and overbold,' for trading with Macbeth in riddles without her, for a 'wayward son' who loves for his own ends. She orders them to meet her at the pit of Acheron in the morning, where Macbeth will come to know his destiny, and plans illusions that will draw him on to his confusion. 'Security is mortals' chiefest enemy.'

context.history: Most editors think this scene (in rhyming tetrameter and calling for a song found in Thomas Middleton's play The Witch) was added after Shakespeare's death, perhaps for a revival.

significance: Hecate states the trap outright: false confidence ('security') will ruin Macbeth. Whether the scene is Shakespeare's or not, it shapes how audiences read the apparitions.
discussionQuestions: Is feeling completely safe ever dangerous? When?
Where does setting appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with fate and free will?

satQuestions.passage:
Have I not reason, beldams as you are,
Saucy and overbold? How did you dare
To trade and traffic with Macbeth
In riddles and affairs of death;
And I, the mistress of your charms,
The close contriver of all harms,
Was never call’d to bear my part,
Or show the glory of our art?
And, which is worse, all you have done
Hath been but for a wayward son,
Spiteful and wrathful, who, as others do,
Loves for his own ends, not for you.
But make amends now: get you gone,
And at the pit of Acheron
Meet me i’ the morning: thither he
Will come to know his destiny:
Your vessels and your spells provide,
Your charms and every thing beside.
I am for the air; this night I’ll spend
Unto a dismal and a fatal end:
Great business must be wrought ere noon:
Upon the corner of the moon
There hangs a vaporous drop profound;
I’ll catch it ere it come to ground:
And that distill’d by magic sleights
Shall raise such artificial sprites
As by the strength of their illusion
Shall draw him on to his confusion:
He shall spurn fate, scorn death, and bear
His hopes ’bove wisdom, grace and fear:
And you all know, security
Is mortals’ chiefest enemy.

segments.script: Most editors think this scene (in rhyming tetrameter and calling for a song found in Thomas Middleton's play The Witch) was added after Shakespeare's death, perhaps for a revival. Hecate states the trap outright: false confidence ('security') will ruin Macbeth. Whether the scene is Shakespeare's or not, it shapes how audiences read the apparitions. Characterization: Hecate scolds the witches and plans Macbeth's ruin through "security" (overconfidence). Structure: The scene is often cut or attributed to Middleton. Diction / vocabulary: Rhyming tetrameter like the witches'. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

objective: Students will summarize what happens in Act III, Scene V (Hecate and the machinery of fate) in 2 sentences and, in a 3-sentence warm-up response, explain how one quoted line from the scene sets up the scene that follows.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: Retell the most important events of “Act III, Scene V” in order, one sentence for each event.
items.lookFor: Hecate angrily scolds the Witches, 'beldams' who are 'saucy and overbold,' for trading with Macbeth in riddles without her, for a 'wayward son' who loves for his own ends. She orders them to meet her at the pit of Acheron in the morning, where Macbeth will come to know his destiny, and plans illusions that will draw him on to his confusion. 'Security is mortals' chiefest enemy.'
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
